doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

chapter: Learning tunes and the dance-gig years
title: John Coates and Phil Woods at the Deer Head Inn
summary: Sitting in with John Coates and Nelson Hill, Phil Woods's strength and tough bandstand manner, and generous mentors.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Oh yes. He’s an author too as well I think.

Oh yeah. He wrote a lot of music for Fred Waring who was across the street, the Pennsylvanian. They had a choral society and they wrote all kinds of arrangements for choral groups all over the world you know. So he was part of that. He wrote. But every weekend he was at the Deer Head. And he’d let us sit in. So here I’d get to play with John Coates and my friend Nelson Hill on saxophone, then I would run as fast as we could to get there and we would play, and then who knows like Phil Woods would show up, you know with his clarinet in his robe, you know to sit in with us and play. It was a great music lesson you know? All his years of experience and the strength of his sound and the conviction, the message he was saying, you know, just make you stand back, you know? You had to listen.

That’s such an interesting thing for you to say, and hard to explain to – like his intent, his message. You feel the need to really listen to what – and I don't know how you can explain how you could do that. Can you do it on purpose or is it just in him?

Well I think both. I think both. If he sensed – well he was a guy, you know that school, that generation of players, if you didn’t know your bridge or something he would humiliate you on the bandstand. You know? He would say nasty things in front of the audience to you, and you would shrink you know, but that’s the way they were you know. They were tough that way. So you didn’t want to play a tune you didn’t know along with him. But yeah, his strength, just all the years and experience he played, you know he was so used to playing on certain chord progressions or not. You know he just knew what to do at the time. He was one of the greatest lead alto players of our time. And him and Quincy Jones especially, did a lot of stuff together. But you know he would be also the kind of guy that would, “Oh check these changes out on this bridge, you should check these changes out.” You know? So he was always teaching as well you know. And I found out with a lot of the great players, they were always willing to give you help. And Dave Liebman was like that, this other saxophone player George Young, Al Cohn gave me opportunities you know. So I’m very lucky you know, to be able to play gigs and be on the bandstand with these gentlemen and move forward. Have that experience, you know?
